items.content:
Over the summer, we have been sprinting on safety priorities; it's more important than ever for capabilities and safeguards to advance together. We have more to do but have made a lot of progress. We are also going to be launching our next model soon.

There is an obvious tension here: on one hand, Astra is very good and we are excited to see what people will build with it. We are proud of our work.

On the other hand, we are clearly in a phase of development where we believe caution is warranted, and we are pacing our progress to ensure that we can meet the safety standards required by new capability levels.

Astra has been done training for a while now and is a significant step forward in both capabilities and alignment. For the models after that, we have been slowing things as needed to ensure that we can do sufficient work on safety and alignment.

AI is getting extremely capable; no one fully understands the consequences of this. Managing the transition to a world with abundant and powerful AI to optimize for safety and benefits to people should be one of the highest priorities in the world. It is our highest priority at OpenAI.

We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us. We know it is much more discordant for other people. And yet, we believe strongly that the world needs to understand where AI is going and how models perform in the real world. More importantly, we believe the world will need aligned AI to manage the future phases of this transition.

An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.

So we hope you enjoy our new model, and we hope the world continues to take what’s happening in AI extremely seriously.

items.content:
One non-model thing I'm very excited we announced today with Fable 5.1 is Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS).

Even if you're not a CEO/CISO, this blog post is a look into how big companies are thinking about AI adoption which is important to understand if you're interested in how AI might diffuse across industry.

Companies are giving agents more and more access to internal systems. With traditional zero data retention, there's been no way to spot patterns in what agents might be doing across sessions on these systems.

EFS is ZDR++. It's ZDR built for a world with agents. A company's data stays in its own cloud, and an automated monitoring layer we built flags risky patterns to its team.

I think of this as an observability and risk mitigation layer for agents. My guess is it will become a standard requirement from enterprises for running increasingly powerful AI on their systems.

items.title:
Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me
items.content:
Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me to pay attention. 

I’m breaking down the key parts of the @RyanGreenblatt tweet on the METR research covering the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

As background: METR is an independent 3P research non-profit that focuses on AI evaluations and risk assessments. They went to the OpenAI offices for 6 days to run these retros. METR takes no funding from AI companies and was not paid to do this research, but they used ~$400,000 in provided OpenAI credits to complete the research. Ryan is Chief Scientist at Redwood Research, who worked with METR on this, and he was in charge of the transcripts. 

This is a sign of what’s to come. 

1) Scale of understanding massive complex systems requires AI because a human can’t read 1300 transcripts, many with millions of tokens, in a few days - big bottlenecks of time and volume 

2) Humans become more reliant on AI for analysis and explanations of complex AI activity 

3) That process will get harder: 

a) AI may stop communicating in natural language either because it’s less efficient than shorthand code (which they used) or activations (numbers) or because AI agents will want to purposefully hide their reasoning from humans…making it harder to understand. 

b) The incidents may (and almost certainly will) get more complex…making it harder to understand. 

c) AI seems likely to get “smarter” and more capable (ex: better at tool handling, fewer errors, more complex orchestration, more clever at staying stealth or going undetected for longer) and may execute more sophisticated hacks…making it harder to understand. 

d) The AI running the investigation already had issues (incomplete, overconfident) and may be even less helpful in the future and could do more on hiding key details, incomplete answers, lying, or not answering…making it harder to understand. 

Reducing urgency and improving testing and prevention may help. Open reports like this one are also helpful to democratize the details (although, we are also democratizing the details for agents to scan). Seems likely we’ll see more open research in this area.

items.title:
OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder
items.content:
OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder all weighed in on X with so much subtly, I had to go Nancy Drew mode and dissect each tweet. 

My translation of each one 👇 

OpenAI - they trust the Cursor team, they don’t trust SpaceX, it’s a “proposal” so maybe this public tweet is a way to gain leverage in the negotiation (note that it came from the company account on a Friday night)

Cursor - seems surprised about the OpenAI tweet, sounds like they want to fight it, goes out of their way to say OpenAI is a small percent of traffic, calls into question their neutrality (though I don’t think the labs call themselves neutral) (and note it came from the CEO, not the company account)

Anthropic - reaffirms the trust in Cursor and reminds us that it’s been years of trust, highlights they’re providing more of the most constrained carrot (compute), takes positive spin on the acquisition by SpaceX (note that it came from founder Tom who we don’t hear from often and not Anthropic account, and note that Cursor CEO reshared) 

Do I think it’ll hold? It’s hard for me to see a world where OpenAI continues to provide model access to a Musk-led company. Maybe if the structure of SpaceX shifts to allow for it, but that’s a big shift. 

Do I think Anthropic got a big PR boost? No, devs are focused on the loss of O, not the maintenance of partnership with A. They care about their own work. 

What’s the theme here? TRUST. How long has the trust been there, who holds the relationship, what hurt it, how to keep it. At the end of the day, all of these companies are led by people.

items.title:
Amazon is shutting down Mechanical Turk in September.

In 2023, a study from academic researchers in Switzerland found t
items.content:
Amazon is shutting down Mechanical Turk in September.

In 2023, a study from academic researchers in Switzerland found that up to 46% of AMT workers were using AI to complete their tasks. 

I can’t imagine that number got any lower, and I wouldn’t be surprised if 2026 numbers were 80%+ if the same study were to run again. 

I remember using AMT for data labeling a decade ago. We would have several labelers label/count each thing, and then look at consensus, variability, and risk of each thing before providing final labels. 

Unless these data labeling companies control the entire environment (ex: Scale AI opens an office that has human labelers come in every day), it’s a ripe opportunity for cheating. Just like asking kids to do their homework without any help from ChatGPT. 

We should assume that, even if they are asked not to do so or even if they sign a contract that they says they shouldn’t, humans outside of controlled environments will use AI to get something done if it gives them an advantage. 

For those of us who have been in AI 10+ years, this feels like a big deal. 

I feel nostalgic for easier AI times sometimes, and then I open up my Monday triage emails and Slacks from Claude Code and Codex and jump right back in.

I was copying and pasting the same boilerplate around and it just didn't feel right.

So I built an open source library
items.content:
I was copying and pasting the same boilerplate around and it just didn't feel right.

So I built an open source library and put it out there.

Months later someone pulled me aside at an event in San Francisco and said they were using it. I asked who they were.

They said Oracle.

I had no company then. No pricing. No contract, no sales team. Twenty years of engineering and a library I had given away.

What I had not understood is that the people with the hardest problems find you first. Not hobbyists. Large enterprises, already in production, before you know they are there.

That is when I knew there was a business in it.

Not a market size. One person at an event telling me the decision had already been made without me.

So what was the signal?

Somebody with real money and real risk had committed before I had.

A lot of founders wait for a permission that never arrives. Go find out who is actually using your thing.

items.title: You pay $20/month for a Claude subscription. But you still hit the limit by 2 pm. I did too, until I understood how Clau
items.content:
You pay $20/month for a Claude subscription. But you still hit the limit by 2 pm. I did too, until I understood how Claude calculates credits: 

It re-reads the entire chat every time you send a prompt. Prompt 30 costs about 31x more than message 1. 

Upload the same PDF to 5 chats & you pay for it 5 times. Run Opus on a grammar check & you pay Opus prices for a Haiku job.

Here are the stupid simple 9 fixes to use every day:

FIX 1. Shrink your files.

Open a Google Doc. Paste the text from your PDF.
Download it as a .md file and upload that instead.
A 15-page PDF costs ~45,000 tokens.
The same text as .md costs ~2,000.

FIX 2. Plan in Chat, then build in Cowork.

In Claude Chat, prompt: "Help me plan a [financial model]. Ask me questions first."
Paste the finished plan into Cowork & say: "Build exactly this."

FIX 3. Let Claude prompt you instead.

A 500-word prompt costs 500 tokens. 
A click costs almost zero.
So prompt: "I want to [TASK] to [SUCCESS CRITERIA]. Ask me questions using AskUserQuestion before you start."

Full guide here: https://t.co/KNO2y4RkYr

FIX 4. Edit your last message.

If you want to correct a mistake, go to your sent prompt, click "Edit" on your message, retype your prompt, and hit Save.
Claude regenerates from that point.

FIX 5. Summarize every 15 prompts chat.

Prompt: "Summarize this entire conversation into a brief." Copy the brief. Paste it as message # 1 in a new chat. Turning 105,000 tokens into 500.

FIX 6. Pick the model before you start.

Open the model dropdown in the chatbox.
Under 30 seconds of thinking? Sonnet.
Execution, multi-step work? Opus.
Brainstorming or solving a complex problem? Fable

FIX 7. Use Projects for repeated files.

Create a Project. Upload your files there once. Every chat inside that Project reads them without re-tokenizing.

FIX 8. Turn off the settings that a task doesn't need.

Go to the tools panel. Turn off Web Search, connectors unless this specific task needs them.
Every idle feature adds tokens.

FIX 9. Batch your asks.

Send "Summarize this, list the key points, and write a headline" as ONE message. Three separate messages make Claude reload the full context three times.

Grab the free guides to copy my full system:
✦ The 27-fixes breakdown: https://t.co/KNO2y4RkYr
✦ The infographic cheat sheet: https://t.co/psB7XxB2Y4

items.content:
There's a fascinating new startup using dogs to detect cancer in human breath

In a new trial, the dogs detected it over 90% of the time!

How it works:

Dognosis has patients breathe into a cotton surgical mask, which is then frozen and shipped to their farm in India.

There, a dog works a line of 10 samples. One beagle breezed past the first five, stopped at the sixth, moved away, came back, and circled it for several seconds.

To her, the whole thing is a game, and the reward is a treat.

But the dog is only half the system. Sensors track each dog's movement, body language, and brain activity.

A probabilistic model then combines signals from multiple dogs, weighted by each dog's historical accuracy, into a single score.

In a study of over 3,000 people, that system caught 90.8% of the real cancers, and correctly cleared 91.3% of the people who didn't have any.

The catch is that this was from a case-control study, where researchers already knew who had cancer (finding rare cases hidden in a healthy population is a harder problem).

BUT a larger trial is running now across 10 Indian hospitals.

If it holds up, we might use dogs to help detect cancer in the future

People ask me what a marketing engineer builds first.

Build a growth repo. Call it Growth OS. It is where your company's marketing memory lives.

Five folders:

1) Customer truth:  sales call notes, support tickets, churn notes, interviews

2) Content engine: founder voice guide, winning hooks, scripts, what performed before

3) Outbound engine: ICP, account research, trigger events, approved angles

4) Creative testing: ad angles, landing page tests, hooks, offers, results

5) Agents: the jobs your AI workers do

Then the prompt changes.

Before: "write me 10 LinkedIn posts"

After: read the customer truth file, read the founder voice file, read the last five posts that drove qualified replies, then draft five new posts about the pains buyers mentioned this week.

The catch: this only works if you stop working in random chats. You ask for 10 posts, you copy one into a doc, and the rest disappears. Next week the AI starts from scratch.

Make the folder today. Put your last sales call in it.

A simple mental framework for how long an agent takes to complete a task:

A task can essentially be broken down into th
items.content:
A simple mental framework for how long an agent takes to complete a task:

A task can essentially be broken down into the number of tokens by the implementation model x its harness needed to achieve it.

Consider a very difficult task, a very smart model might need to iterate 10x before it gets it right, and might require 10mn toks.

A less smart model might need to iterate 1000x before it gets it right, and might require 1bn toks. 

A dumb model will never get it right even if you let it iterate 1mn times, and will require an infinite toks.

--
Between the very smart model and the less smart model above, if the very smart model outputs tokens at 10 tok/s and the less smart model outputs tokens at 1000 tok/s, they actually complete the task at the same time.

So it's not JUST about intelligence.

The same thing is true about costs, it's temping to look at $/mn toks and state that a model is cheaper than another, but what you're actually interested in is the $/difficult task for the work you are doing. 

The "more expensive" model might end up using $100 for $10/mn toks for 10mn toks to complete the task, while the "less expensive" model might end up using $1000 for $1/mn toks for 1bn toks to complete the task.

--
Lastly, there are some tasks where anything LESS than frontier (e.g. Fable) literally cannot iterate towards the correct solution.

This is why frontier models continue to be very attractive even if cheaper models are available. 

Until a supermajority of "very hard" tasks can be solved by OSS models, OpenAI and Anthropic will likely continue winning over more and more prosumers.

--
Bonus: There are some domains that are "so difficult", which is another way of saying that the solution space is so far away from the training data available to the models (e.g. quant finance), that you will literally need to provide iterative feedback for the model to arrive at a reasonable solution.

One of the best repos to build as a marketing engineer is a customer truth file.

1) Make a file called what the market is telling us.md

Good morning everyone 🌞 

August did not feel like a victory lap. It felt like the first month the work finally started
items.content:
Good morning everyone 🌞 

August did not feel like a victory lap. It felt like the first month the work finally started to compound.

For years @BeldexCoin built privacy into the stack when most of the industry treated it as a toggle. Wallet. Messaging. Routing. Identity. Quiet infrastructure. Not a narrative.

Then the ground shifted. AI agents started moving value, talking, and acting onchain. Suddenly the question was not do users want privacy? It was can an agent hold an identity, pay, and compute without leaking the whole decision tree?

That is the month they closed.

On 15 August they closed an $8M strategic round led by Sigma Capital, with NTC, Nxgen, Digital Consensus Fund, and EAK Ventures. Not a marketing raise. Runway to turn a live privacy ecosystem into infrastructure other people can build on: SDKs, an extension wallet, confidential assets, an EVM-compatible sidechain, encrypted agent identities, FHE, and quantum-resistant consensus.

The rest of August was less glamorous and more honest.

The new Beldex Bridge passed a Hacken audit, findings got fixed, and we put native BDX back onto BNB Smart Chain. BelNet 1.4.1 shipped on Android. We published the VRF-based PoS research that the next consensus hardfork will sit on. MiCA Whitepaper V2.0 went live. The extension wallet left the private repo.

None of that is the finish line. June already taught them what happens when a bridge or a consensus edge case is treated as good enough. They do not get to skip that lesson.

Privacy is no longer a feature you bolt on after the architecture is done. If the next wave of Web3 and AI is going to touch money, messages, and memory, encryption has to be the default before a single byte hits the network.

That is what August bought them: time to build it that way.

Onward.

items.content:
A warning to all designers

I'm seeing a dangerous trend on LinkedIn and X, and I need to call it out.
 
In trying to prove you can "design and build with AI," designers are oversimplifying the process. And it's backfiring badly.

What I'm seeing:

"I built an entire app in seconds with AI."
 "You don't need to give any input, AI handles everything."
 "Designed and shipped in hours with no effort."
 
Imagine you're a potential client reading that. Why would you hire a designer if it sounds like they did nothing? Like AI did all the work?

Here's the reality:

Anyone who's actually built something with AI knows the truth. The work is immense.
 
You need to:
 
- Write detailed PRDs and briefs
- Know which AI tools solve which problems
- Run commands in the terminal
- Manage API tokens and costs
- Make countless design iterations
- Test, refine, validate
- Make critical decisions at every step
 
This isn't automation. This is strategy disguised as simplicity.

The damage you're doing:

By making it sound effortless, you're training clients to think designers are obsolete. You're undercutting your own value.

What you should actually communicate:

"I used AI strategically to accelerate execution while maintaining my standards. Here's the thinking behind the decisions. Here's what I refined. Here's the work that went into this."
 
That's the message that gets clients excited. That's what justifies the rate.

Remember:

Your critical thinking is still essential. Your judgment still matters. Your ability to see what AI missed, that's irreplaceable.
 
Don't sell yourself short trying to sound impressive. Show the actual work. Show the thinking.

items.content:
Cross chain bridges have often introduced a new trust assumption into otherwise decentralized systems. @BeldexCoin is trying to address that at the cryptographic level with a bridge design using Threshold Signature Scheme and Distributed Key Generation.

Instead of giving one custodian or a small group complete control over the signing process, the design distributes that authority across participants. No single party would hold the entire signing solution.

The setup is intended for transfers between the Beldex native chain and BNB Smart Chain. It forms part of the extended protocol roadmap, following development and audit work on a basic bridge.

The important part is where the trust sits. Rather than depending mainly on an organization to control the bridge, TSS and DKG aim to distribute control through the underlying cryptographic structure.

For a privacy focused network expanding into cross chain transfers, keeping that control distributed is an important consideration. It is less about adding another bridge and more about reducing the points where trust can become concentrated.

@EthraShip is building its ecosystem piece by piece, with real maritime activity providing the foundation for what comes next.

Three operational vessels under Ethra Invest are already generating economic activity across global trade routes, while Sea Verity is being developed to create more reliable and confidence scored vessel intelligence.

The community portal is now live, giving participants a way to complete missions, earn Ethra Points, and build reputation. At the same time, development of the first RWA pilot is underway, with structured, eligibility based access to vessel backed maritime assets.

Sea Verity remains the bigger vision, bringing together maritime signals, contributors, verification, and evidence to create a more reliable intelligence layer.

For me, the interesting part is the steady development across the ecosystem. Real vessels, a growing data network, community participation, and RWA infrastructure are all being built alongside each other.

Most people already generate plenty of health data through devices like Apple Watch, Oura Ring, Whoop, and other wearables. The problem isn’t necessarily getting more signals.

The harder part is understanding what those signals mean and knowing what to actually do with them. That is where @sleepagotchi’s agentic AI approach comes in.

Instead of leaving sleep and recovery data sitting inside an app, the idea is to connect those signals, identify personal patterns, and turn them into useful insights that can guide the next step.

The bigger vision extends beyond sleep into wellness, nutrition, and shopping. More context gives the AI more information to work with and potentially makes its recommendations more relevant to the individual.

The future of wellness probably isn’t about endlessly buying more devices. It’s about having smarter systems that can learn from the data we already generate and help turn that information into better decisions every day.

items.content:
Yes, it can be distressing to cut open orchard fresh apples and find it this way.

I immediately get emails, msgs, comments, abuse - we have scammed fraud, shipped rotten apples, how do we sleep at night cheating people...

Been dealing with this vexed issue called - core rot - since 2023.

I remember the first time I saw pictures like this from one lot and went back to the farmer. Even the farmer couldn't understand why it happened at such a scale. Apples had passed external visual inspection two times - how did it happen?

There was not much AI back then. So had to work through apple diseases and literature to zero in.

The climate pattern has changed since 2023. We had the worst pre and main monsoon ever that year and was an absolute disaster for apples. Our company revenue fell by half. It rained so hard the apple tree leaves just gave up and dropped. And what apples were left majority suffered core rot.

The higher heat and warm rain during apple flowering season below 7500 ft has become a challenge. Core rot happens when bacteria and fungi that should not exist in that season penetrate the flower and the young apple bud through its partially open stem. Water seeps through capillary action. Then they sleep because the growing fruit insulates them from heat and growing foliage provides shade. Also a growing apple is mostly starch and has optimum sugar only when mature.

The apple looks nice and red - normal from outside. If you cut it open after plucking like we do - nothing will be visible. Perfect.

Apples will get packed and travel down to mainland India. The core temp of the apples will briefly cross 24-25C somewhere in a transport chain. The devil will awaken in a bed with high sugar yummy apple pulp.

The core will rot. Ethylene gas will get generated in the box, some bruised apples will join the party 🥳. A box meets a smelly watery end.

The vexed thing about this is - across an orchard very less % trees or in some cases only a few branches will get affected. But the effect on a harvest is exponential in the logistics chain.

Many times customers will dump an entire box on finding one apple like this as it's psychologically difficult for them and we have to refund/replace in full.

At least for us it's individual box cases...

It's more brutal in wholesale mandis. There is an informal credit system there. Typically 7-10 days. So a farmer will sell his lot of apples to a buyer on 7-10 day credit with the trader standing 'informal' guarantee for the price. Buyer on the 5-6th day to his horror finds entire boxes disintegrating. Payment default. There have even been cases recently where rotting lots have been brought and dumped back in the mandi. Leads to overall price inflation of the fruit. Ask anyone working as a trader in a mandi and they will tell you how nasty this business gets.

We absorb such losses, transport damages everything in our company. When a farmer had his parchi cut with us, payment is transferred and end of transaction. Goodwill though gets paid back in kind, till today, whenever we put up cases like these, we usually get some volunteer compensation stock next year. Relationships get built through weathering the good and the bad.

Is your money really safe when a chain like $INJ is halted and exploited?

@injective halted block production for 3 hour
items.content:
Is your money really safe when a chain like $INJ is halted and exploited?

@injective halted block production for 3 hours 42 minutes on August 31.

An attacker walked away with roughly $4.9M.

Here's what actually happened, and why the official response doesn't hold up.

→ The exploit

Injective's market_id is built by concatenating oracle type, ticker, denom, and provider with no separators. An attacker engineered a collision between an INJ-denominated insurance fund and a USDC-denominated binary options market.

When the no-price refund path fired, the system paid the USDC shortfall out of the raw INJ balance. Insurance capital became the exit.

→ The part that should bother you more than the exploit

Injective made its core repos, injective-core and injective-chain, private earlier this year. The stated reason was that a closed codebase is harder for attackers to find bugs in.

You didn't need the source to find this one. Obscurity didn't buy safety, it just meant users found out less.

→ The response

While the chain sat frozen and insurance funds were being drained, the official account posted twice. An AI agent SDK announcement.

A bridge promotion. Zero mention of the halt. CEO Eric Chen later called it "an upgrade, not a halt" and said funds are safe.

> Block explorer: 3h42m of dead blocks after an active exploit.

> CEO: just an upgrade.

> Insurance fund: down $4.9M.

Pick which one you trust.

Exchanges weren't confused as Upbit flagged it, Bitget and MEXC froze deposits and withdrawals same day.

This is not "the L1 got hacked." It's a module level bug the chain itself executed, then a comms response that tried to rename the event.

What's your line for when "the chain is safe" stops meaning anything?

items.content:
Just finished mapping out the entire AI tooling landscape.

The data is fascinating, but the real story is in the connections.

Here’s my unfiltered take: The "Agentic AI" category is a misnomer. That’s the brain (the LLMs). The real "Agent" is the nervous system coordinating all the other parts.

Let me walk you through the blueprint of a modern AI stack:

1. The Brain (Foundation Models)
We've got deep pockets here. It’s no longer just OpenAI vs. Anthropic. The rise of open-weight models (Llama, Mistral) and the infrastructure to run them (Ollama, vLLM) is democratizing the core intelligence. The choice here defines your system's "personality."

2. The Nervous System (Orchestration & RAG)
This is where the magic happens. LangGraph and CrewAI are dominating the multi-agent workflow space. But look at Microsoft AutoGen and AWS Strands, the cloud giants are building their own moats. They're not just connecting to a database; they are routing tasks between specialized agents.

 3. The Memory (Short & Long-term)
This is the hardest problem to solve. Tools like Memo and Zep are building "stateful" agents, while LangGraph Memory is trying to make it native to the graph. The secret sauce? It's not just about what you remember, but how you retrieve it. This is where Vector DBs (Pinecone, Qdrant) and Graph DBs (Neo4j) intersect.

4. The Eyes (Embedding & Retrieval)
RAGFlow and GraphRAG are pushing the boundaries beyond keyword search. They are moving towards semantic understanding and knowledge graphs. The choice of BGE vs. Voyage AI for embeddings is becoming a strategic decision based on domain specificity.

5. The Immune System (Security & Guardrails)
Production is scary. NVIDIA NeMo and Guardrails AI are the bouncers at the club, ensuring outputs stay on-brand and safe. If you don't have a "Guardrails" layer, you don't have a production system.

6. The Vital Signs (Observability)
You can't fix what you can't see. LangSmith and Langfuse are the dashboards for the AI brain. They’re moving beyond logging to tracing the chain of thought. Ragas and TruLens are specifically for evaluating the retrieval quality—a crucial win condition.

 7. The Hands (Agent SDKs)
Finally, we have the execution layer. OpenAI Agents SDK vs. LangChain Agents vs. PydanticAI. The trend is clear: frameworks are getting lighter and more pythonic. The goal is to move from "building a robot" to "writing a script."

The Big Picture:
This isn't just a spreadsheet of tools. It’s a modular brain. The winners won't be the ones with the best single component, but the ones who can chain them together seamlessly.

We are moving from "Prompt Engineering" to "System Architecture."
